conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because of nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning and just started vomiting. I couldn’t stop. I’ve been having these episodes more often lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have Type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis, correct? And a gastric pacemaker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had the pacemaker for a few years. It helps a little, but not like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was high when you arrived—306—and your anion gap was elevated, which means mild ketoacidosis. That’s likely from not keeping food or insulin down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I did take my Lantus last night and a little Humalog this morning, but I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you some insulin and fluids in the ER. You’re on IV fluids now to rehydrate and we’ll keep an eye on your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so dehydrated. My mouth feels dry, and I’m dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Vomiting a lot can cause volume depletion. Your heart rate is high—139—which is likely from that and the mild DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but not critical. We’re treating it with fluids and your usual metoprolol. We switched it to IV for now since you can’t take pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My blood pressure has been up and down too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. You were hypertensive in the ER, but it’s improved. We gave IV enalaprilat earlier and will switch back to your lisinopril when you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want my blood pressure spiking again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it closely. For your nausea, we’re giving IV Zofran and Reglan, and your scopolamine patch is on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That patch helps a little. I’ve had Botox injections before for my gastroparesis—those helped too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ll plan for you to follow up with GI soon. They may repeat the Botox if it worked before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. I’ve been admitted so many times for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you were in the hospital last week for DKA. It sounds like your gastroparesis is getting harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I can’t keep insulin down, so my sugars go high, and then I get sicker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you insulin through shots now. Your anion gap has already improved from 20 to 10, which is good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow if your nausea improves. We’re also treating your GERD with IV omeprazole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been off my esomeprazole because I wasn’t taking pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it by mouth when you can swallow. One more thing—we did a chest X-ray to check your port and make sure there’s no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your port is fine, lungs are clear, and your gastric stimulator is in place. No free air, so no perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea is better today, I hear. You kept down some apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes! First thing in days. I still feel queasy, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood sugar is stable—around 150. We switched your IV fluids to D5NS since your sugars came down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s D5NS?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s saline with dextrose—sugar—to prevent your levels from dropping too low now that you’re not as dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, got it. And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on your home Lantus—28 units at night—and Humalog on a sliding scale. We’re watching your response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad we’re getting back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—we got your urine culture back. It showed some bacteria, including Group B Strep. Even though you don’t have urinary symptoms, we’re starting ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I had a UTI. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. With diabetes, we treat even asymptomatic infections to prevent complications. It’s just a 4-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You had one episode of vomiting this morning when your sugar was high, but you tolerated lunch well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your anion gap is normal, heart rate is down to 88, and you’re eating. We’re sending you home with your usual meds plus cipro for 4 more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up with GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In four days. They’ll discuss repeating the Botox injection. Keep using your anti-nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you so much for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if vomiting returns or your sugars go above 300. Otherwise, see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: you’re alert, walking fine, and your vitals are stable. All set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.
